title: How to Plan Retirement as a Couple With Big Income Differences
description: Optimizing Social Security and savings when one spouse earns more.
content:
When one spouse earns $150,000 and the other earns $30,000 (or $0), retirement planning requires a 'Team' strategy. The instinct is often to split bills proportionally, but this leaves the lower earner with little retirement savings. To maximize household wealth, you must leverage the tax code to equalize benefits. Strategies like Spousal IRAs, strategic Social Security claiming, and optimizing the 401(k) match can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your joint net worth.

Key Takeaways

  • The Spousal IRA: A non-working (or low-earning) spouse can have an IRA funded by the high earner's income. This doubles your IRA space to $14,000/year.
  • Super-Funding the High Earner: If the lower earner's job doesn't offer a 401(k), the household should live on the lower salary and direct 100% of the high salary's surplus into the high earner's 401(k) max.
  • Social Security Strategy: The higher earner should delay claiming until 70 to maximize the survivor benefit. The lower earner can claim early (62) to provide cash flow now.
  • Life Insurance Gap: The lower earner is financially vulnerable if the high earner dies young. You need 10-15x the high earner's income in Term Life insurance to protect the survivor.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Survivor Benefit' in Social Security dictates that a widow(er) keeps the higher of the two checks. Maximizing the high earner's record is the best form of longevity insurance for the lower-earning spouse.

The Unequal Earner Protocol

Stop thinking 'My Money' vs 'Your Money'. It is 'Our Future'.

1. Maximize Tax Space

High Earner: Max 401(k) ($23k) + Catch-Up ($7.5k).
Low Earner: Max 401(k) (if available). Spend High Earner's paycheck to subsidize Low Earner's payroll deduction.
Goal: Get $60k+ into tax-advantaged accounts annually.

2. Roth Conversions

If the high earner retires early, use the 'Gap Years' to convert their massive Traditional 401(k) into Roth IRAs. This balances the tax buckets for both spouses.

3. Legal Protections

Ensure beneficiary designations are correct. If the high earner dies, assets should pass to the spouse instantly, bypassing probate. A Revocable Living Trust is often the best tool for this.

Communication Tactics

  1. The 'No-Questions' Allowance: Give each spouse an equal 'Fun Money' transfer every month (e.g., $500). This equalizes lifestyle even if incomes are different.
  2. Joint Savings: Emergency funds and house funds should be joint. If the low earner has no liquidity, they feel trapped. Shared liquidity builds trust.
  3. Long-Term Care: The lower earner (often the wife) tends to live longer. Ensure the plan accounts for 5 years of nursing care for the survivor.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if we divorce?

Retirement assets accumulated during marriage are generally split 50/50 (QDRO). You are building a joint asset regardless of whose name is on the account.

Does the non-working spouse get Medicare?

Yes. If the working spouse qualifies (40 quarters of work), the non-working spouse qualifies at 65 on their record. Premiums are the same.

Can we retire at different times?

Yes. The high earner might retire at 55, while the low earner works to 65 for health insurance benefits. This is a common 'Health Care Bridge' strategy.
